The Intrinsic Conditional Auto-Regressive (ICAR) Model in Stan

ICAR Model Specification

  • Conditional specification: multivariate normal random vector \(\mathbf{\phi}\) where each \({\phi}_i\) is conditional on the values of its neighbors

  • Joint specification rewrites to Pairwise Difference, \[ p(\phi) \propto \exp \left\{ {- \frac{1}{2}} \sum_{i \sim j}{({\phi}_i - {\phi}_j)}^2 \right\} \]

  • Each \({({\phi}_i - {\phi}_j)}^2\) contributes a penalty term based on the distance between the values of neighboring regions

  • \(\phi\) is non-identifiable, constant added to \(\phi\) washes out of \({\phi}_i - {\phi}_j\)

    • A sum-to-zero constraint identifies and centers \(\phi\)

Stan implementation

Encode neighbor information as graph edgeset, i.e. pairs of indices for neighbors \(i, j\):

data {
  int<lower = 0> N;  // number of areal regions
  int<lower = 0> N_edges;  // number of neighbor pairs
  array[2, N_edges] int<lower = 1, upper = N> neighbors; // column-wise adjacent
  ...

Use Stan’s sum_to_zero_vector to identify phi

parameters {
  sum_to_zero_vector[N] phi; // spatial random effects
  ...

Use Stan’s vectorized operations to compute log probability density

model {
  target += -0.5 * dot_self(phi[node1] - phi[node2]);
  ...

New York City Neighbor Graph

New York city consists of several islands; only the Bronx is part of the mainland; Brooklyn and Queens are part of Long Island, Manhattan and Staten Island are large islands with hundreds of census tracts, and City Island, Roosevelt Island, and the Rockaways are smaller, comprised of 1, 2, and approximate 20 census tracts, respectively.

This is a problem for the ICAR model, which operates on a fully connected graph (single component)

nyc_nbs = poly2nb(nyc_geodata, queen=FALSE)

ICAR Model: poisson_icar.stan

Coding the neighbor graph

  • \(N \times N\) Adjacency matrix
    • Entries \((i,\ j)\) and \((j,\ i)\) are 1 when regions \(n_i\) and \(n_j\) are neighbors, 0 otherwise
  • Undirected graph: regions are vertices, pairs of neighbors are edges
    • Encoded as edges - 2 column matrix, each row is a pair of neighbors \(({n_i}, {n_j})\)

The Stan ICAR model uses the latter. Encode neighbor information as a graph.

  • Nodes are indexed from 1:N.
  • Edges indices are stored in a 2 x N array
    • each column is an edge
    • row 1: index of first node in edge pair, \(n_i\)
    • row 2: index of second node in edge pair, \(n_j\)
  int<lower = 0> N;  // number of areal regions
  // spatial structure
  int<lower = 0> N_edges;  // number of neighbor pairs
  array[2, N_edges] int<lower = 1, upper = N> neighbors;  // node[1, j] adjacent to node[2, j]

Coding the ICAR component

The joint distribution of the ICAR model is expressed as the pairwise difference between neighboring regions in the neighbor graph.

\[ p(\phi) \propto \exp \left\{ {- \frac{1}{2}} \sum_{i \sim j}{({\phi}_i - {\phi}_j)}^2 \right\} \]

The joint distribution is non-identifiable; adding any constant to all of the elements of \(\phi\) leaves it unchanged, therefore we add the constraint \(\sum_{i} {\phi}_i = 0\).

  • Use Stan’s constrained parameter type sum_to_zero_vector to identify the joint distribution.
  sum_to_zero_vector[N] phi; // spatial effects
  • Use Stan’s vectorized operations to compute log probability density:
   target += -0.5 * dot_self(phi[node1] - phi[node2]);  // ICAR prior

Putting it all together

This file is in directory stan/poisson_icar.stan.

poisson_icar_model_file = file.path('stan', 'poisson_icar.stan')
cat(readLines(poisson_icar_model_file), sep="\n")
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  array[N] int<lower=0> y; // count outcomes
  vector<lower=0>[N] E; // exposure
  int<lower=1> K; // num covariates
  matrix[N, K] xs; // design matrix

  // spatial structure
  int<lower = 0> N_edges;  // number of neighbor pairs
  array[2, N_edges] int<lower = 1, upper = N> neighbors;  // columnwise adjacent
}
transformed data {
  vector[N] log_E = log(E);
  // center continuous predictors 
  vector[K] means_xs;  // column means of xs before centering
  matrix[N, K] xs_centered;  // centered version of xs
  for (k in 1:K) {
    means_xs[k] = mean(xs[, k]);
    xs_centered[, k] = xs[, k] - means_xs[k];
  }
}
parameters {
  real beta0; // intercept
  vector[K] betas; // covariates
  sum_to_zero_vector[N] phi; // spatial effects
  real<lower=0> sigma; // overall spatial variance
}
model {
  y ~ poisson_log(log_E + beta0 + xs_centered * betas + phi * sigma);
  beta0 ~ std_normal();
  betas ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ std_normal();
  target += -0.5 * dot_self(phi[neighbors[1]] - phi[neighbors[2]]);  // ICAR prior
}
generated quantities {
  real beta_intercept = beta0 - dot_product(means_xs, betas);  // adjust intercept
  array[N] int y_rep;
  {
    vector[N] eta = log_E + beta0 + xs_centered * betas + phi * sigma;
    y_rep = max(eta) < 26 ? poisson_log_rng(eta) : rep_array(-1, N);
  }
}

pois_icar_data <- list(
  N = nrow(brooklyn_geodata),
  y = as.integer(brooklyn_geodata$count),
  E = as.integer(brooklyn_geodata$kid_pop),
  K = 4,
  xs = design_mat,
  N_edges = ncol(brooklyn_nbs_adj),
  neighbors = brooklyn_nbs_adj
)

Model is compiled (as needed) on instantiation

pois_icar_mod = cmdstan_model(stan_file=poisson_icar_model_file)

pois_icar_fit = pois_icar_mod$sample(data=pois_icar_data, parallel_chains=cores, refresh=0)

Model Checking

Visualizing the ICAR component

To see the spatial structure of the data, we plot the covariance matrix of phi. We expect neighboring regions to be correlated, and distant regions to be uncorrelated. To do this, we have written a helper function, plot_icar_corr_matrix.

y_rep_icar <- as_draws_matrix(pois_icar_fit$draws("y_rep"))
plot_icar_corr_matrix(y_rep_icar, 'ICAR correlation matrix')

The long diagnonal edge shows evidence of high correlation between adjacent regions, in contrast to the lack of any distinctive pattern along the short edges or interior of the plot.

Posterior predictive checks

ppc_central_interval(y_rep_icar, pois_icar_data$y)
[1] "y total: 745, ct y is within y_rep central 50% interval: 695, pct: 93.29"
ppc_y_yrep_overlay(y_rep_icar, pois_icar_data$y,
                     'Poisson + ICAR model PPC\ny (blue dot) vs. y_rep (orange 50% central interval, grey full extent)')

Model Comparison: Poisson + ICAR vs. Poisson vs. Poisson + RE

The Poisson-ICAR model falls into the category of “non-factorized models”, for which simple leave-one-out cross-validation fails to hold, due to the fact that observations depend on other observations from different spatial units in addition to the dependence on the model parameters Doing cross-validation would require recoding the model, and then re-fitting is \(N\) times, once per omitted observation. Therefore, we compare summary statistics, visualizations, and model runtimes.

Poisson model (with centered predictors)

pois_re_mod = cmdstan_model(stan_file=file.path(
  'stan', 'poisson_ctr_preds.stan')) 
pois_re_fit = pois_re_mod$sample(data=pois_icar_data, parallel_chains=cores)

Discussion

The Poisson + RE model has somewhat better predictive coverage because the random effects component theta effectively accounts for the overdispersed nature of the data. However, visualization of the ICAR component demonstrates that the ICAR component does a good job of capturing the spatial structure of the data and also provides good predictive performance. In the next notebook, we show how to combine both components into the BYM2 model.
